findings.description: SHEET-MARK-007's literal text defines the SubCent boundary on the RAW reading — 'a non-positive numeric price reading (0.0 or negative)'. All three A-sketches implement exactly that: A1/A2 check `reading <= 0.0` (or `v <= 0.0`) on the raw f64 before any conversion; A3 does the same and then separately converts to cents. The real code (`price_to_cents`, lib.rs:362-385) does NOT gate on the raw reading being non-positive — it gates on the POST-ROUNDING integer cents value: `numerator = (price_usd*100*SCALE).round()`, `cents = round_half_to_even(numerator, SCALE)`, then `if cents <= 0 { Err(SubCent) }`. This is strictly broader: it also catches a strictly-positive raw reading that rounds down to 0 cents — pinned by the test `subcent_positive_price_is_degraded_anomaly_not_zero` (`price_to_cents(0.0001) == Err(SubCent)`). A literal, faithful implementation of the spec's own wording (as A3 does, checking `v <= 0.0` then converting `(v*100.0).round_ties_even()`) would instead silently return `Mark(0)` for 0.0001 — directly contradicting the same EARS sentence's closing clause, 'so a bad reading never silently understates ... value.' All three B-runs independently surface this as a named, deliberately-coded rule beyond the literal text (B1 SHEET-MARK-F; B2 'a positive sub-cent price that rounds down to 0'; B3 item 3(c)) — the same gap seen from both sides: the spec names the trigger as a property of the reading, the code (and its own `SubCent`/'sub-cent anomaly' naming) actually defines it as a property of the rounded cents.

The exact rounding algorithm for the successful-conversion path — scale by `SCALE = 1_000_000`, round via `pt_core::round_half_to_even` (banker's rounding, ties to even), pinned at the cent boundary by `usd_price_converts_to_cents_round_half_to_even` (`1.005 -> Cents(1_00)`, `1.015 -> Cents(1_02)`) — is never stated by SHEET-MARK-007, which only speaks to the degraded-anomaly boundary, not how a valid positive reading is rounded. All three B-outputs pin this precisely (SCALE, round-half-to-even, the two tie examples); none of the A-sketches address it (A1/A2 explicitly place conversion out of scope; A3 invents an arbitrary 'round_ties_even' placeholder and flags it as such). Likely governed by a sibling EARS ID (the doc-comment calls `round_half_to_even` 'the project's single canonical rounding site'), not 007 itself, so weight this below finding 1.

In `read_marks` (lib.rs:847-869), a `PriceReading::Numeric` that fails `price_to_cents` (either `SubCent` or the numeric-`Permanent` case) is recorded straight into `degraded` with NO fallback to a previously-cached-good `Mark` for that symbol — contrast with `PriceReading::Transient`, which explicitly carries `prior` forward (and is tested doing so: `transient_keeps_prior_mark_and_retries_degrades_only_after_window`). SHEET-MARK-007's 'never as a mark' clause says nothing about whether a stale-but-known-good prior price may substitute for today's bad reading; the code's real answer — no, discard outright and degrade — is surfaced by all three B-runs (B1 SHEET-MARK-E; B2 'NOT carry forward any prior cached mark'; B3 item 4, 'reserved for the transient/timeout path only') with no A-side counterpart, since a single-reading classifier has no notion of 'prior' at all. Note: the general degrade-excludes-mark behavior is well tested, but the specific combination of 'a populated prior mark exists AND today's Numeric reading is SubCent/non-finite' is not directly exercised by any test in marks.rs — the claim is accurate but code-level, not test-pinned for that exact combination.

`price_to_cents` performs a second, redundant finiteness check on the SCALED intermediate (`price_usd * 100.0 * SCALE`) after the initial raw-reading check, to catch a finite-but-astronomically-large reading that overflows to `±∞` during scaling — also routed to `Permanent`. SHEET-MARK-007's 'a non-finite reading (NaN/±∞)' language presumes the raw reading itself is the object being checked, and says nothing about a post-scaling overflow trigger. All three B-runs note this defensive double-check (B1 SHEET-MARK-C, B2, B3 item 2 'redundantly'), but no test in marks.rs exercises an actual overflow-magnitude price, so this is a code-only claim, not a test-pinned one — weakest of the four findings.

notes: Read both real files in full (lib.rs 1-1027, tests/marks.rs 1-314) before comparing. The A-side unanimously agrees on: check-order (finite before non-positive, correctly recognized by all three as load-bearing for NaN), -0.0 treated as non-positive, +inf/-inf both folding into Permanent, and — critically — gating the SubCent boundary on the raw reading rather than any converted value (this last point is the seed of finding 1). The differences among A-runs (A1 carries the raw reading in the anomaly payload, A2/A3 don't; A3 alone attempts the actual f64->Cents conversion inline, incidentally exposing the rounds-to-zero bug) are incidental scope choices, not disagreement on the core classification semantics, so I rated A agreement 'high' rather than 'medium'. The B-side is unusually tight: all three independently reconstruct the exact same constant (SCALE=1_000_000), the exact same rounding rule and tie examples, the exact inclusive cents<=0 boundary (explicitly citing the 0.0001 rounds-to-zero case), and the same no-prior-carry-forward semantics for numeric-degrade vs. transient. Given B's high internal agreement and the fact that finding 1 is traceable from literal A-side spec-fidelity AND independently from B-side code-fidelity to the identical underlying boundary-definition mismatch, BD-DRIFT is the right call rather than B-ONLY-DRIFT — dropping to B-only would understate that a faithful spec-only implementation (A3) concretely produces the wrong, value-understating answer the spec itself was written to prevent.
